scene-u01-pnew1-5.name: text#5
scene-u01-pnew1-5.text: First use the best path to assign each observation to a state, then count directly to get new probabilities

scene-u01-pnew1-6.name: text#6
scene-u01-pnew1-6.text: How to read: in each sequence the top row is the observed color and the bottom row the state given by the best path (each state covers one run); the right gives four counts on the path and the formulas.

scene-u01-pnew1-8.name: text#8
scene-u01-pnew1-8.text: Round 0 segmentation: red to state 1, blue to state 2, green to state 3

scene-u01-pnew1-92.name: text#92
scene-u01-pnew1-92.text: Assign step: cut observations into runs owned by each state

scene-u01-pnew1-94.name: text#94
scene-u01-pnew1-94.text: Update step: re-estimate parameters from each run

scene-u01-pnew1-95.name: text#95
scene-u01-pnew1-95.text: Alternate until the cost stops changing; like $k$-means clustering, hence segmental $k$-means

scene-u01-pnew1-99.name: text#99
scene-u01-pnew1-99.text: Hard assignment (integer counts on the best path) versus soft weighting (expected counts); usually simpler and faster to converge.

scene-u01-pnew1-101.name: text#101
scene-u01-pnew1-101.text: Four counts on the best path

scene-u01-pnew1-117.name: text#117
scene-u01-pnew1-117.text: Total visits to state $i$, the emission denominator

scene-u01-pnew2-5.name: text#5
scene-u01-pnew2-5.text: One round raises the total cost from $-11.4928$ to $-4.6821$; one more and it stops

scene-u01-pnew2-6.name: text#6
scene-u01-pnew2-6.text: How to read: the left is step 1 (counting on the best paths of both sequences); the right is step 2 (new parameters) and the total cost after re-finding paths; larger is better.

scene-u01-pnew2-52.name: text#52
scene-u01-pnew2-52.text: Emissions are $0$ and $1$ because there are only two sequences and $13$ observations; real systems need enough data and smoothing for unseen pairs.

scene-u01-pnew2-79.name: text#79
scene-u01-pnew2-79.text: Emissions: each state has one color, so all are $1$

scene-u01-pnew2-100.name: text#100
scene-u01-pnew2-100.text: Number line: total cost $D$, larger is better

scene-u01-pnew2-104.name: text#104
scene-u01-pnew2-104.text: Paths and counts do not change, so neither does $D$.

scene-u01-pnew2-106.name: text#106
scene-u01-pnew2-106.text: Costs and counts computed by code, checked

scene-u01-pnew3-5.name: text#5
scene-u01-pnew3-5.text: A wrong hard assignment cannot be fixed: the flatter start stops at $-6.4082$, worse than $-4.6821$

scene-u01-pnew3-6.name: text#6
scene-u01-pnew3-6.text: How to read: the left shows total cost from two starts (larger is better; green: good start, orange: flatter start), below is the round-0 segmentation of the flatter start; the right gives uses and limits.

scene-u01-pnew3-40.name: text#40
scene-u01-pnew3-40.text: Both jump at round $1$, then stay

scene-u01-pnew3-41.name: text#41
scene-u01-pnew3-41.text: Round-0 segmentation of the flatter start (sequence 1):

scene-u01-pnew3-63.name: text#63
scene-u01-pnew3-63.text: The second blue goes to state $3$ (rose box); with a wrong hard assignment, the next counts only confirm the error

scene-u01-pnew3-69.name: text#69
scene-u01-pnew3-69.text: Simpler and faster than Baum-Welch; it states which state owns each observation, enabling segmentation, and is a good starting point for Baum-Welch.

scene-u01-pnew3-73.name: text#73
scene-u01-pnew3-73.text: Hard assignment gets stuck: a poor start stops at a worse fixed point; run from several starts, or refine Viterbi results with Baum-Welch.

scene-u01-pnew3-77.name: text#77
scene-u01-pnew3-77.text: Zero probabilities: real systems need enough data and smoothing for unseen pairs.

scene-u01-pnew3-81.name: text#81
scene-u01-pnew3-81.text: "Viterbi re-estimation and Baum-Welch give the same parameters" is wrong: one uses integer counts, the other probability-weighted expected counts.

scene-u01-pnew3-83.name: text#83
scene-u01-pnew3-83.text: [Added] Costs of the flatter start computed by code
